sorular.konu: Why RAG: LLM limitations and the retrieval decision
sorular.soru: A class assistant must decide how to answer the question 'Is room A015 free right now?' Which path is appropriate?
secenekler: LLM alone: it is general knowledge, so the model already knows the answer
RAG: the answer is a fact written in class documents such as the syllabus
Agentic RAG: if the documents fall short, the agent searches the web
Tool/API call: the answer is live data that appears in no document
sorular.aciklama: Current room occupancy is live data that is written in no document; it should be routed to a tool call such as a calendar API. The RAG option is misleading because retrieval only suits facts already written in documents; real-time status is not in the index.

sorular.konu: RAG vs. Long Context vs. Fine-Tuning
sorular.soru: A team wants its support bot both to adopt the organization's formal correspondence style and to relay a return policy that changes every week correctly. Using the usual decision rule (new behavior → fine-tune, new knowledge → RAG), which mechanism is appropriate?
secenekler: Fine-tuning only: both style and policy are baked into the weights
Long context only: the policy documents are added to the prompt on every query
Fine-tuned model + RAG: behavior lives in the weights, knowledge in the index
Continued pretraining: the model is adapted from scratch with new domain data
sorular.aciklama: The decision rule says 'new behavior → fine-tune, new knowledge → RAG, both → fine-tuned model + RAG'; style is a behavior, while a weekly-changing policy is knowledge. Fine-tuning only is misleading because fine-tuning is generally regarded as 'weak at adding new facts' and it would require retraining every week.

sorular.soru: For Contextual Retrieval, an LLM call is made for every chunk, and each call contains the same document. The engineer builds the prompt in the order 'chunk + whole document' and sees no benefit from prompt caching. What is the problem?
secenekler: The varying part (the chunk) comes first, so the prefix does not match and the KV cache cannot be used
The cache stores only output tokens; the input document is therefore reprocessed from scratch on every call
The document exceeds 50–100 tokens, so it goes over the cache limit and is skipped automatically
Each call carries a different chunk, so caching by definition does not work in this scenario at all
sorular.aciklama: The rule is 'fixed part first, varying part last; the prefix must match exactly'; when the chunk is placed first, every call's prefix differs and the document's KV cache cannot be reused. The last option is misleading: this scenario (a different chunk per call, the same document) is exactly the ideal use of caching; the problem is not that the chunk changes but where it is placed.

sorular.konu: RAG vs. Long Context vs. Fine-Tuning
sorular.soru: In the 'Lost in the Middle' experiment, accuracy followed a U-shaped curve with respect to the position of the document containing the answer (≈76% at position 1, ≈54% at position 10). Which RAG design choice does this finding justify?
secenekler: Enlarging the context window so that all retrieved chunks fit into a single prompt without any selection
Keeping fewer chunks through reranking and placing the best one at the start of the prompt
Shrinking the chunk size so that more chunks can be retrieved within the same token budget
Raising the overlap ratio so that facts at chunk boundaries are not lost during indexing
sorular.aciklama: Because evidence in the middle is often overlooked, the usual remedy is 'rerank, keep fewer chunks, put the best first'. Retrieving more chunks is misleading: as the prompt grows, evidence drifts to the middle, and 'needle in a haystack' misses also increase with length.

sorular.konu: RAG pipeline: offline indexing and online querying
sorular.soru: A class assistant answers the question 'When is the YZM5109 midterm in 2026?' with last year's date (17 November 2025). In the logs, the similarity scores of the 2025 and 2026 syllabus chunks look almost equal. In a typical RAG pipeline (retrieve, rerank, generate), which is the most direct fix?
secenekler: Increasing the embedding dimension to separate the two chunks in vector space
Reducing the chunk size to isolate the date sentence on its own
Adding a cross-encoder reranker to move the correct year's chunk to the top
Applying a metadata filter such as year = 2026 in the retrieve step
sorular.aciklama: Without a year filter, the 'Midterm: 17 Nov 2025' chunk can receive almost the same score and reach the LLM; the fix is a metadata filter in the vector DB. A reranker is misleading because both chunks are equally semantically relevant to the 'midterm date' question; the distinguishing information lies in the metadata, not the text.

sorular.konu: Embeddings, cosine similarity, and indexing hyperparameters
sorular.soru: A 2,500-token document is split with the sliding window method using typical values (chunk size 500 tokens, overlap 100 tokens). If each new chunk repeats the last 100 tokens of the previous one, how many chunks are produced?
sorular.aciklama: With an overlap of 100, the window advances 400 tokens per step: the starts are 0, 400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2000, and the last chunk covers the range 2000–2500; 6 chunks in total. The answer 5 ignores the overlap (2500/500), while 7 rounds 2500/400 up and overlooks that the first chunk covers 500 tokens.

sorular.soru: In a moon.md example, recursive chunking never cuts sentences, but one chunk contains both the sentence about the Moon receding and the '## Apollo 11' heading. How does document-based chunking solve this problem, and what new limitation does it introduce?
secenekler: It cuts where similarity between neighboring sentences drops; it adds the cost of one embedding per sentence
It cuts at a fixed number of characters; it risks splitting numbers and words in the middle
It makes each section a single chunk; overly long sections still need to be split separately
It repeats the boundary text in the next chunk; it enlarges the size of the index
sorular.aciklama: Document-based chunking follows the heading structure and makes each section a single chunk; its cost is that 'long sections still have to be split'. The first option describes semantic chunking: it also cuts at topic shifts, but it does so by looking at sentence embeddings rather than document structure.

sorular.konu: Embeddings, cosine similarity, and indexing hyperparameters
sorular.soru: Using the definition of cosine similarity, what is the similarity of the vectors q = (1, 1, 0) and d = (0, 1, 1)?
sorular.aciklama: Since q·d = 1 and ‖q‖ = ‖d‖ = √2, cos = 1/(√2·√2) = 0.50. The answer 1.00 takes only the dot product and skips dividing by the norms; 0.71 (1/√2) divides by only one of the norms.

sorular.konu: Evaluation: retrieval metrics, golden set, correctness vs. faithfulness
sorular.soru: What is the purpose of adding questions whose answers are not found in the documents, such as 'Who grades the projects?', to the golden set?
secenekler: To obtain more gold evidence rows for measuring the retriever's recall at different cutoffs
To measure the system's ability to say 'I don't know' when appropriate (abstention)
To verify the quality of LLM-generated questions through a human review of each sampled item
To keep the hold-out set separate from the questions used during prompt and parameter tuning
sorular.aciklama: For unanswerable questions the correct answer is 'I don't know'; these rows feed the abstention metric. The first option is misleading because the gold evidence for these questions is 'not in the documents'; they do not contribute to recall measurement.

sorular.konu: Dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval; vector databases and ANN
sorular.soru: A system using only dense (bi-encoder) retrieval often returns Apollo 13 chunks for the query 'Apollo 11 crew'; on the other hand, the query 'How far away is the Moon?' finds the 'Distance: 384,400 km' chunk without trouble. Which statement explains both behaviors together?
secenekler: Dense search captures paraphrase but is not discriminative on exact names and numbers
Dense search relies on word matching; it captures paraphrase only through IDF weighting
The embedding dimension is small; if enlarged, both names and paraphrases are separated
ANN indexes give approximate results; exact search would have filtered out the Apollo 13 chunks
sorular.aciklama: Dense search's strength is capturing the 'how far ≈ distance' paraphrase and its weakness is confusing Apollo 11 with 13; the remedy is hybrid search that also adds BM25. The ANN option is misleading: ANN only finds nearest neighbors approximately and does not fix the fact that the Apollo 11 and 13 vectors are close to begin with.

sorular.konu: Dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval; vector databases and ANN
sorular.soru: In a hybrid search example, 'Exam schedule' is 1st and 'Midterm rooms' is 2nd in the semantic list; in the keyword list, 'Midterm rooms' is 1st and 'Exam schedule' is 3rd. After RRF, why does 'Midterm rooms' move to the top of the hybrid list?
secenekler: RRF applies a higher weight coefficient to the BM25 list than to the dense list
RRF normalizes the cosine and BM25 scores and takes their arithmetic mean
RRF keeps only chunks present in both lists and drops the others
RRF sums the reciprocals of the ranks in each list; 1/1 + 1/2 exceeds 1/1 + 1/3
sorular.aciklama: The RRF score is computed as Σ 1/(k + rank); the total for Midterm rooms (ranks 2 and 1) is greater than that for Exam schedule (ranks 1 and 3). The score normalization option is misleading: RRF looks only at ranks, not raw scores, which is how it can combine cosine and BM25 scores of different scales; also, Syllabus and Class calendar remain in the hybrid list, so it does not keep only common chunks.

sorular.soru: Although a cross-encoder produces more accurate scores than a bi-encoder, why is it used only on the top-k candidates rather than in the initial search over 1 million chunks?
secenekler: It reads the query and chunk together, so it requires a separate model call for every pair
Its output is a single vector, so it is too high-dimensional to be stored in an ANN index
It compares chunks only at the keyword level, so it misses paraphrase
It forces the entire model to be retrained whenever a new document is added
sorular.aciklama: A bi-encoder precomputes chunk vectors offline and compares them with the query via cosine; a cross-encoder reads each (query, chunk) pair together, so there is nothing to precompute and the cost grows with the number of pairs. The second option is misleading: a cross-encoder outputs a relevance score directly, not a vector; the problem is not vector size but that nothing can be precomputed.

sorular.soru: In the golden set analysis, in most failed questions the correct chunk is absent from all 20 candidates returned by the retriever. According to the standard RAG failure-diagnosis scheme, which intervention should be made first?
secenekler: Adding a stronger cross-encoder reranker to rescore the candidates
Adding an 'answer only from the context' instruction and a mandatory citation rule to the prompt
Revisiting chunking, hybrid search, or query rewriting
Raising top-n from 3 to 5 to send more candidates to the prompt
sorular.aciklama: If the correct chunk is not in the top-20, the problem lies in retrieval; in this case the recommendation is to fix retrieval with 'chunking, hybrid, rewrite'. A reranker is misleading because it only reorders its input: it cannot move up a chunk that is not among the candidates. Increasing top-n fails for the same reason.

sorular.konu: Evaluation: retrieval metrics, golden set, correctness vs. faithfulness
sorular.soru: In a golden set of three questions, the first relevant chunk is found at ranks 1, 2, and 4, respectively. By the standard definition, what is the approximate MRR?
sorular.aciklama: MRR = (1/1 + 1/2 + 1/4) / 3 = 1.75 / 3 ≈ 0.58. The answer 0.43 is misleading: it takes the reciprocal of the mean rank (7/3), whereas the definition first takes the reciprocal for each question and then averages. 0.33 is just the fraction of questions found at rank 1 (Hit@1).

sorular.konu: Evaluation: retrieval metrics, golden set, correctness vs. faithfulness
sorular.soru: In an evaluation example, the context contains only the chunk '[1] midterm topics: chapters 1–6', yet the model answers 'The midterm is on 16 November 2026', and this date is in fact correct. In RAGAS terminology, how is this answer classified?
secenekler: Correct but not faithful: the context does not say this; the model used its memory
Correct and faithful: since the answer is correct, it is deemed consistent with the context too
Faithful but not correct: the model stayed true to the context but was mistaken
Abstention: the model stated that the context is insufficient and left the question unanswered
sorular.aciklama: Correctness is compared against the ground truth, while faithfulness is compared against the retrieved context; the date is correct but [1] does not say it, so the answer is unsupported, which is explained as 'model used memory'. 'Correct and faithful' is misleading: correctness does not imply faithfulness, and the main point is that these two criteria must be measured separately.

sorular.konu: Advanced RAG: HyDE, CRAG, Multi-hop, GraphRAG, Agentic and Multimodal RAG
sorular.soru: In an Advanced RAG pipeline, which of the following techniques aims to improve the query itself BEFORE the retrieval step?
secenekler: Context compression: chunks are summarized and shortened before entering the prompt
Cross-encoder reranking: candidates are rescored by reading them together with the query
CRAG: an evaluator grades the retrieved documents as Correct / Ambiguous / Incorrect
HyDE: a hypothetical answer written by the LLM is embedded and used for the search
sorular.aciklama: In the diagram, the 'before retrieval' step fixes the query (rewrite, expand, HyDE); HyDE embeds a fake answer instead of the short question and searches for real documents near it. CRAG is misleading: although its name suggests 'corrective', its evaluator runs after retrieval, to grade the retrieved documents.

sorular.konu: Advanced RAG: HyDE, CRAG, Multi-hop, GraphRAG, Agentic and Multimodal RAG
sorular.soru: For the question 'Which exams are in A011 on 16 November?', vanilla RAG finds only the YZM5109 midterm while GraphRAG also finds the YZM5112 quiz. What is the source of this difference, and what is GraphRAG's cost?
secenekler: More chunks are retrieved with a larger top-k; the cost is a longer and more expensive prompt
The graph neighbors of the A011 node are traversed; the cost is one LLM pass per chunk
BM25 matches the 'A011' token exactly; the cost is blindness to paraphrase
The agent finds extra documents through web search; the cost is additional tool calls on every question
sorular.aciklama: The relevant information is spread across different documents; GraphRAG builds an entity–relation graph and walks from the A011 node to neighboring exams via local search, and its cost is 'one LLM pass over every chunk'. Enlarging top-k is misleading: vector search looks for 'similar text', and since the second document is not semantically similar enough to the query, it may still rank low.

sorular.konu: RAG security, knowledge conflicts, and application-specific design
sorular.soru: A class assistant that also indexes PDFs uploaded by students answers the question 'When is the midterm?' with 'The midterm has been cancelled'; the retrieved chunk contains the sentence 'Ignore all previous instructions…'. What is the name of the problem and the primary defense?
secenekler: Knowledge conflict; the model should be told to prefer the context over its memory
Hallucination; the answer should be checked against the context with the faithfulness metric
Lost in the middle; the correct chunk should be moved to the start of the prompt with a reranker
Indirect prompt injection; retrieved text should be treated as data, not as orders
sorular.aciklama: The hidden instruction in the retrieved document was treated by the model as a command; this is called indirect prompt injection and the defense is 'retrieved text is data, not orders', indexing only trusted sources, and filtering by user permissions. Knowledge conflict is misleading: a 'prefer the context' instruction would here make the model trust the poisoned chunk even more.
